name: Stoke Hall
use: Largest residence hall: 593 students; floors 2–3 mostly upper-division, floors 5–8 first-year
builtText: two Garrison Ave wings 1965; third wing 1966; dedicated Nov 16–17, 1966

renovations.what: Upgraded first-floor gaming lounge and newly updated fifth-floor study lounge (date not given)

facts.text: At 83 feet, Stoke was the university's first high-rise; two wings facing Garrison Avenue were built in 1965 and the third in 1966.
Designed by Leo Provost and built by Davison Construction on the site of Ballard Hall, which was demolished in 1961 to make way for it.
Named for Harold Walter Stoke, UNH president 1944–1947, during an enrollment surge that more than tripled enrollment.
UNH's largest residence hall, with 593 students and two resident assistants on every floor; it has an elevator and a gender-inclusive restroom on every floor.

verdict: UNH's first high-rise: a curving nine-storey 1966 slab housing 593 students; social, loud, dated, no A/C.
notes: Old row's dramatic condition claims (20–30 sinks broken 2022–23, fall-2025 vandalism, moldy shower ceilings, Buildings of New England 'graceful' quote, Her Campus 2016 quote, MyDorm grade D) were NOT re-verified in this pass; a targeted search found nothing. Old row 'built 1965' corrected to 1966 completion (1965 for first two wings). Photos: eight-storey brick-and-white-concrete-banded slab with strip windows, institutional; a double room shows vinyl floor, bare painted block walls and wood loft furniture. Licensed photos: 2021 shows the eight-storey courtyard facade, two long brick-and-white-spandrel wings framing a glazed central tower; 2013 shows the curving wing on Garrison Avenue. Big, institutional, dated; window ribbons suggest ordinary room light.
judgeNotes: Photos show a monumental but heavy banded slab. 04.jpg kept: its series identification matches the other views (brick end tower, banded wings).
